title: A transcript names a student
summary: A teaching team responds to an unintended disclosure in a practice-class transcript.

facts.text: A teaching assistant reports that a practice transcript was shared with a small course team after class.
The teacher sees a line naming a student and describing a disability. The exercise uses invented people and does not contain the line itself.
The accessibility adviser knows a student may need support but has not seen the transcript or a diagnosis.
The teaching assistant says the transcript link was available to eight course staff; download history is unavailable.
The accessibility adviser learns that the affected student wants to keep participating without repeatedly explaining their needs.
The retention setting and incident-reporting owner are unknown; check the institution's actual rules before deciding what to report or delete.
The course lead asks for a containment and communication plan before the next class, including who owns each action.
The adviser recommends asking the student privately about immediate support needs without requiring them to disclose a diagnosis again.
Compare the applicable UAE personal-data framework with the institution's incident policy and any other jurisdiction involved; the scenario does not establish a legal reporting deadline.

title: Captions fail before a workshop
summary: A teaching team must provide access when a planned captioning option fails.

facts.text: The live caption service for an English-language university workshop is unavailable shortly before it begins.
The teacher can pause or change the activity but does not know which alternatives each student prefers.
The accessibility adviser knows that at least one attendee depends on captions; the attendee has not agreed to disclose their identity to the class.
An accessible written activity and a trained note-taker are available; their suitability has not yet been confirmed with the affected attendee.
A third-party caption tool is available, but its audio retention and data-processing terms have not been checked.
The adviser can privately ask the attendee which immediate option is usable and whether postponement would be preferable.
The department asks for a fallback plan that assigns owners, avoids singling out attendees, and can be tested before future workshops.
Check the applicable UAE higher-education requirements and institutional accommodations procedures. School-specific guidance may offer context but may not govern this university workshop.
Before a vendor processes audio, the privacy team still needs the data terms and institutional approval route.

title: Feedback mistaken for a grade
summary: Students confuse AI-generated practice feedback with an official grading decision.

facts.text: A student asks why a practice tool gave their presentation a failing grade, although the exercise was meant to be formative.
The teacher finds that the feedback display used a numerical score without clearly saying that it was not an official grade.
The accessibility adviser has heard that the display was difficult to interpret with a screen reader, but has not yet tested it.
The course team confirms that the official gradebook did not receive the practice score.
The student says the score discouraged them from seeking help; the adviser requests a usable explanation and an accessible way to challenge the feedback.
The team has not established which student data the feedback provider retained or whether it can correct stored results.
The course lead asks for a correction to affected students and a human-owned plan for reviewing feedback before the next activity.
Compare UAE AI ethics guidance with UNESCO and England education guidance as contextual references; verify local applicability and avoid treating any guidance as an automatic grading rule.
Test any revised explanation and challenge route with assistive technology and invite feedback from affected students.
